image.e: From Middle English ymage, borrowed from Old French image, from Latin imāgō (“a copy, likeness, image”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eym-; the same PIE root is the source of imitari (“to copy, imitate”); see imitate.
image.g: A visual or other representation of the external form of something in art.

imagery.e: From Middle English ymagerie, from Middle French imagerie; equivalent to image + -ry.
imagery.g: The work of one who makes images or visible representation of objects.

imagination.e: From Middle English ymaginacioun, from Old French imaginacion, ymaginacion, from Latin imāginātiō. Equivalent to imagine + -ation.
imagination.g: The image-making power of the mind; the act of mentally creating or reproducing an object not previously perceived; the ability to create su

imagine.e: From Middle English ymagynen, from Middle French imaginer, from Latin imāginor, from imāginem, the accusative singular of imāgō (“a copy, likeness, image”).
imagine.g: To form a mental image of something; to envision or create something in one's mind.

imbibe.e: From Middle English imbiben, from Latin imbibō, from im- + bibō (“to drink”) (whence also beverage), from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₃-, whence also potable, potion.
imbibe.g: To drink (used frequently of alcoholic beverages).

imitate.e: Borrowed from Latin imitātus, perfect active participle of imitor (“to copy, portray, imitate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
imitate.g: To follow as a model or a pattern; to make a copy, counterpart or semblance of.

imitator.e: From French imitateur, derived from Latin imitātor, equivalent to imitate + -or.
imitator.g: A person who imitates or apes another.

immediate.e: From Old French immediat (French immédiat), borrowed from Late Latin immediātus (“without in-between, moderation”), from Latin in + mediātus, perfect passive participle of mediō (“to halve, to be in the middle”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from medius (“middle”). By surface analysis, im- + mediate.
immediate.g: Happening right away, instantly, with no delay.

immediately.e: From Middle English immediatly, equivalent to immediate + -ly.
immediately.g: In an immediate manner; instantly or without delay.

immense.e: From Middle English immens, inmens, from Old French immense, from Latin immensus, from in- (“not”) + mensus (“measured”).

imminent.e: From the present participle of Latin imminēre (“to overhang”), from mineō ("to project, overhang"), related to minae (English menace) and mons (English mount).
imminent.g: About to happen, occur, or take place very soon, especially of something which won't last long.

immortal.e: From Latin immortālis, from prefix im- (“not”) (from in-) + mortālis (“mortal”) (from mors (“death”), combining form mort- + adjectival suffix -alis), equivalent to im- + mortal. The term referring to the Persian soldiers was a Calque of Ancient Greek ἀθάνατος (athánatos).
immortal.g: Not susceptible to death; living forever; never dying.

immortality.e: From Middle English immortalitee, immortalite, from Old French immortalité, from Latin immortālitās. Morphologically immortal + -ity.

immovable.e: From Middle English immevable, immoveable. Equivalent to im- + movable.
immovable.g: Incapable of being physically moved: fixed.

immune.e: From Middle English, from Middle French immun, from Latin immūnis (“exempt from public service”), from in- (“not”) + mūnus (“service”).

immutability.e: Borrowed from Middle French immutabilité, itself borrowed from Latin immūtābilitās. By surface analysis, immutable + -ity.
immutability.g: The state or quality of being immutable; immutableness.

immutable.e: From Middle English immutable, from Latin immūtābilis (“unchangeable”); im- + mutable.
immutable.g: Unable to be changed without exception.

impale.e: From Middle French, from Medieval Latin impālāre, from Latin palus, whence also pale.
impale.g: To pierce (something) with any long, pointed object.

impart.e: From Middle English imparten, borrowed from Middle French impartir, empartir, from Late Latin impartiō, impertiō, from im- (“in”) + Latin partiō (“divide”).
impart.g: To give or bestow (e.g. a quality or property).

impartial.g: Treating all parties, rivals, or disputants equally; not partial; not biased.

impatient.e: From Old French impacient (modern French impatient), from Latin impatiēns. By surface analysis, im- + patient.
impatient.g: Restless, short of temper, and intolerant of delays.

impede.e: Borrowed from Latin impediō (“to shackle”), from pēs (“foot”) (compare pedestrian).
impede.g: To get in the way of; to hinder.

impediment.e: From Middle English impediment, borrowed from Latin impedimentum.
impediment.g: A hindrance; that which impedes or obstructs progress; impedance.

impenitent.g: Not penitent; specifically (Christianity), not repenting of one's sins; unrepentant.

imperious.e: From Latin imperiōsus (“mighty, powerful”), from imperium (“command, authority, power”).

imperishable.g: Not perishable; not subject to decay; enduring permanently.

impetuous.e: From Middle English impetuous, from Old French impetueux, from Late Latin impetuōsus (“violent”), from Latin impetus (“attack, violence”).
impetuous.g: Making arbitrary decisions, especially in an impulsive and forceful manner.

implacable.e: From Middle English implācāble (“immitigable, unappeasable”) from Old French implacable (“harsh, unrelenting; implacable”) (modern French implacable), from Latin implācābilis (“unappeasable, implacable; irreconcilable”), from im- (variant of in- (prefix meaning ‘not’)) + plācābilis (“placable; appeasing, moderating, pacifying, propitiating.
implacable.g: Not able to be placated or appeased.

implead.g: to sue in court, raise an action against a defendant

implement.e: Borrowed from Late Latin implēmentum (“a filling up”), from Latin impleō (“to fill up”).
implement.g: To bring about; to put into practice; to carry out.

implore.e: PIE word h₁én The verb is borrowed from Middle French implorer (modern French implorer (“to beg, plead, implore”)), or directly from its etymon Latin implōrāre, the present active infinitive of implōrō (“to beseech, entreat, implore; to appeal to, pray to”), from im- (a variant of in- (intensifying prefix)) + plōrō (“to cry out.
implore.g: To beg or plead for (something) earnestly or urgently; to beseech.

import.e: From Middle English importen, from Old French emporter, importer, from Latin importō (“bring in from abroad, import”, verb), from in (“in, at, on; into”) + portō (“to carry, bear; convey”).
import.g: Something brought in from an exterior source, especially for sale or trade.

import.e: From Italian importare, and French importer, from Latin importō.
import.g: To be important; to be significant; to be of consequence.

importance.e: From Middle English importaunce, from Middle French importance, from Medieval Latin importantia. By surface analysis, import (“to be important”) + -ance.
importance.g: The quality or condition of being important or worthy of note.

important.e: From Middle English important, from Medieval Latin important-, importāns. By surface analysis, import (“to be important”) + -ant.
important.g: Having relevant and crucial value; having import.

importunity.e: From Late Middle English importunitie, importunyte (“insistence, persistence; grievance; hardship, trouble; inappropriateness (?)”), from Anglo-Norman importunité, and Middle French importunité (“persistent demand; hardship, trouble; something difficult or troublesome.
importunity.g: Constant and insistent demanding or proposing, especially if regarded as annoying or upsetting; also, the character of such behaviour; (coun

impossible.e: From Middle English impossible, equivalent to im- + possible.
impossible.g: Not possible; not able to be done or happen.

impotent.e: From Old French impotent, from Latin impotēns, from in- (expresses negation) + potēns (“powerful”).
impotent.g: Lacking physical strength or vigor; weak

impoverish.e: From Middle English empoverishen, impoverishen, empoverischen, enpoverisshen, Anglo-Norman empoveriss-, from Old French empoverir, from em- + povre, from Latin pauper (“poor”) (English poor).

impression.e: From Old French impression, from Latin impressio. Equivalent to impress + -ion.
impression.g: The indentation or depression made by the pressure of one object on or into another.

imprison.e: From Middle English imprisonen, emprisounen, emprisonen, from Old French emprisonner. Equivalent to im- + prison.
imprison.g: To put in or as if in prison; confine somebody against their will.

imprisonment.e: From Anglo-Norman emprisonement, from Old French emprisonnement.
imprisonment.g: A confinement in a place, especially a prison or a jail, especially as punishment for a crime.

improvement.e: From Anglo-Norman emprouwement. By surface analysis, improve + -ment.
improvement.g: The act of improving; advancement or growth; a bettering

improvise.e: From French improviser; ultimately from Latin improvisus. Not related to improve.
improvise.g: To make something up or invent it as one goes on; to proceed guided only by imagination, intuition, and guesswork rather than by a careful p

impudent.e: From Middle English impudent, originally meaning immodest, shameless, from Latin impudēns (“shameless”), ultimately from in- + pudere (“to feel shame”).
impudent.g: Not showing due respect; bold-faced, impertinent.

impulse.e: Borrowed from Middle French impulser, from Latin impulsus.
impulse.g: A thrust; a push; a sudden force that impels.

impulsive.e: Borrowed from Middle French impulsif, from Latin impulsivus.
impulsive.g: Having the power of driving or impelling; giving an impulse; moving; impellent.

impure.e: From Middle French impur, from Latin impūrus.

impurity.e: From impure + -ity. From Middle French impurité, from Latin impuritas.
impurity.g: The condition of being impure; because of contamination, pollution, adulteration or insufficient purification.

impute.e: Borrowed from Middle French imputer, from Latin imputō (“to bring into the reckoning, charge, impute”).
impute.g: To attribute or ascribe (responsibility or fault) to a cause or source.
